title: The Growth-Rate Ladder
summary: The seven complexity classes you must recognise instantly, the code shape that produces each, and what they cost at real input sizes — including how to read the target complexity straight off the constraints.

slides.markdown:
There are about seven complexity classes you will ever quote in an interview, and each one has a **code shape** that produces it. Recognising the shape is faster and more reliable than deriving the bound from scratch.

The ladder, cheapest to most expensive:

**O(1) → O(log n) → O(n) → O(n log n) → O(n²) → O(2ⁿ) → O(n!)**

By the end of this topic you should be able to glance at a loop nest or a recursive branch and name the class without thinking, and — the part that actually wins interviews — read the *target* complexity off the problem's constraints before you write any code.

slides.subTitle: The bottom three rungs
slides.markdown:
**O(1) — constant.** Work doesn't depend on n at all. Array indexing, a hash lookup, pushing onto a stack, arithmetic. Shape: no loop over the input.

**O(log n) — logarithmic.** Each step throws away a *fraction* of what's left, usually half. Binary search, balanced-BST descent, heap sift-up. Shape: a loop where the index halves (`lo = mid + 1`) rather than increments.

**O(n) — linear.** Touch each element a constant number of times. A single scan, a max-finding pass, one traversal of a linked list. Shape: one loop over the input, with O(1) work inside.

The reason log n is so powerful: doubling the input adds **one** step. Going from a thousand to a billion items takes binary search from ~10 comparisons to ~30. Not 10 to 10,000,000 — 10 to 30.

slides.subTitle: The middle rungs
slides.markdown:
**O(n log n) — linearithmic.** The signature of divide-and-conquer: split the input into halves (log n levels), do linear work at every level. Merge sort, heapsort, and "just sort it first" preprocessing all live here. Shape: a recursive halving plus a linear merge, *or* a sort call inside your solution.

**O(n²) — quadratic.** Two nested loops over the same input, or comparing every pair. Bubble/insertion/selection sort, the naive "check all pairs" scan. Shape: `for i … for j …` over the same collection.

**O(n³) — cubic.** Three nested loops. Naive matrix multiplication, Floyd-Warshall all-pairs shortest paths.

Watch for the **hidden sort**: a candidate writes one loop, calls `sorted()` inside it, and reports O(n). That's O(n² log n). Any library call in a loop carries its own complexity into yours.

slides.subTitle: The rungs you must escape
slides.markdown:
**O(2ⁿ) — exponential.** Every element gives a binary choice: take it or don't. Generating all subsets, naive recursive Fibonacci, brute-force subset-sum. Shape: recursion that branches **twice** and shrinks n by one.

**O(n!) — factorial.** Every ordering of the input. Generating all permutations, brute-force travelling salesman. Shape: recursion that branches n ways at depth 1, n−1 ways at depth 2, and so on.

The practical ceiling is brutally low: 2ⁿ is fine to about n = 20–25, and n! to about n = 10–11. At n = 20, 2ⁿ is a million; at n = 50 it exceeds the number of grains of sand on Earth.

If your first idea is exponential, that's normal — say so, then look for the escape: memoization, pruning, or a greedy/DP reformulation. Naming your brute force *and* its complexity before optimizing is exactly what interviewers want to see.

slides.sectionTitle: All seven curves on one chart
slides.markdown:
Plotted together, the classes separate into three visual families:

- **Flat-ish:** O(1) and O(log n) barely rise. On any realistic axis they hug the bottom.
- **Steady:** O(n) is a straight line; O(n log n) is a line that bends up gently — close enough to linear that in practice "sort it first" is usually affordable.
- **Walls:** O(n²) curves up sharply, and O(2ⁿ) and O(n!) go vertical almost immediately — at any scale where n² is still readable, the exponentials have already left the chart.

That last point is the one to internalise: the gap between quadratic and exponential is far larger than the gap between constant and quadratic.

slides.subTitle: Find a value in 1,000,000 items
slides.markdown:
Same job, three data layouts, three classes:

| Approach | Complexity | Steps at n = 1,000,000 | Cost paid up front |
|---|---|---|---|
| Scan an unsorted list | O(n) | ~1,000,000 | none |
| Binary search a sorted array | O(log n) | ~20 | one O(n log n) sort |
| Hash-map lookup | O(1) avg | ~1 | O(n) build + extra memory |

The complexity of the *lookup* is only half the story — each faster lookup is bought with preprocessing.

That gives you the standard decision rule: **one lookup, don't preprocess. Many lookups, preprocess.** Sorting to enable binary search pays for itself after roughly log n searches; building a hash map pays off after a handful. This is the trade-off an interviewer is probing when they follow up with "and what if we query this a million times?"

Read the shape, not the code:

```python
def a(nums):                      # O(1) — no loop over n
    return nums[0] if nums else None

def b(nums, target):              # O(log n) — range halves each step
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if nums[mid] == target: return mid
        if nums[mid] < target: lo = mid + 1
        else: hi = mid - 1

def c(nums):                      # O(n) — one pass
    return max(nums)

def d(nums):                      # O(n log n) — sort dominates the scan
    s = sorted(nums)
    return s[len(s) // 2]

def e(nums):                      # O(n²) — nested over the same input
    return [(x, y) for x in nums for y in nums if x + y == 0]
```

The tells: no loop → constant. Index halving → log. One loop → linear. A sort → linearithmic. Nesting → multiply.

slides.sectionTitle: What each class costs at real n
slides.subTitle: Assuming 10⁸ simple operations per second
slides.markdown:
Rough wall-clock, at roughly 100 million operations per second — a fair modern estimate:

| n | O(n) | O(n log n) | O(n²) | O(2ⁿ) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 100 | instant | instant | instant | ~10¹³ years |
| 10,000 | instant | instant | ~1 s | — |
| 1,000,000 | ~10 ms | ~200 ms | ~3 hours | — |
| 100,000,000 | ~1 s | ~27 s | ~300 years | — |

Two things to take away. First, **O(n log n) is barely worse than O(n)** at any size you'll meet — the log factor is 20 at a million, 27 at a hundred million. Sorting is almost always affordable.

Second, **O(n²) falls off a cliff between 10⁴ and 10⁶**. That single row is why "can you do better than quadratic?" is the most common follow-up in a coding interview.

slides.sectionTitle: Reading the target off the constraints
slides.markdown:
Interview problems state a bound on n, and that bound tells you which class the interviewer expects. Working backwards from ~10⁸ operations:

| Constraint | Expected complexity |
|---|---|
| n ≤ 10–12 | O(n!) or O(2ⁿ) — brute force is intended |
| n ≤ 20–25 | O(2ⁿ) — subsets, bitmask DP |
| n ≤ 500 | O(n³) — triple loop is fine |
| n ≤ 5,000 | O(n²) |
| n ≤ 10⁶ | O(n log n) — sort or heap |
| n ≤ 10⁸ | O(n) or O(log n) — single pass, no sort |

Use this out loud: *"n goes up to a million, so I need n log n or better — that rules out the pair-wise scan, so I'll sort or use a hash map."*

That one sentence shows you can size a solution before writing it, which is a distinctly senior habit.

O(log n) looks unimpressive next to O(1) on paper, and O(n log n) looks meaningfully worse than O(n). At real input sizes, neither gap is what it appears.

- **log₂(10⁹) ≈ 30.** A balanced BST lookup in a billion-row index is thirty comparisons. Chasing O(1) instead of O(log n) is rarely where your wins are — which is why B-trees, not hash tables, back most database indexes: the log factor is cheap and you get ordered range scans for free.
- **Going the other way**, an "optimization" from O(n log n) to O(n) that adds a hash map can lose on real data, because the log factor you removed was worth 20 and the constant you added was worth more.

The mistake is treating the ladder as a strict ranking of speed. It's a ranking of **growth**. Adjacent rungs are often decided by constants, not by the class.

slides.sectionTitle: Multiples and log bases are noise
slides.markdown:
Three simplifications people get wrong in both directions:

- **O(2n), O(n/2), and O(n + 500) are all just O(n).** Constant multiples and additive constants drop. Two separate passes over the array are still linear — walking the array twice does *not* make it quadratic.
- **The log base doesn't matter.** log₂n and log₁₀n differ by a constant factor (about 3.3), which the notation drops. Writing O(log₂ n) is not wrong, just noisy.
- **But O(n + m) is not O(n).** If the two variables are genuinely independent — two arrays, or nodes and edges — collapsing them hides real information. Keep both.

The rule underneath all three: drop what a faster machine could absorb (constants, bases), keep what depends on the input (distinct size variables, growth terms).
